definition: Stubbornly resisting authority, guidance, or control.
example: The trainer struggled with a recalcitrant horse.
nuance: Recalcitrant often involves resistance to authority, not any disagreement.
prompt: A committee refuses an agreed procedure.
options: The recalcitrant members repeatedly refused to follow the agreed rules.
The recalcitrant members complied readily with every instruction.
Recalcitrant meant the members had never received instructions.
The members were recalcitrant because they were very quiet.
reasons: Persistent refusal illustrates resistance to control.
Ready compliance is the opposite of resistance.
Lack of instructions does not establish defiance.
Quietness alone says nothing about resistance.

practice.prompt: A babysitter is trying to get a toddler ready for bed.
options: The recalcitrant toddler could recall every word of his favorite bedtime story without any help.
The recalcitrant toddler politely asked for one more song, then lay down as soon as it ended.
The recalcitrant toddler kept refusing to put on his pajamas despite the babysitter's patient coaxing.
The recalcitrant toddler cheerfully brushed his teeth and climbed into bed the moment he was asked.
reasons: This treats the word as if it came from recall. It is about defiance, not memory.
A polite request followed by going along with the routine shows no real defiance.
He keeps saying no to the adult in charge even when she asks gently, which is stubborn defiance.
Doing what he is told right away is cooperation, the reverse of stubborn resistance.
